Survey design, weights and pooling

Source: vignettes/survey-design.Rmd
survey-design.Rmd
library(bdhs)
library(survey)
#> Loading required package: grid
#> Loading required package: Matrix
#> Loading required package: survival
#> 
#> Attaching package: 'survey'
#> The following object is masked from 'package:graphics':
#> 
#>     dotchart

The BDHS is a stratified two-stage cluster sample. In the first stage, enumeration areas (clusters) are drawn within strata defined by division and urban/rural residence. In the second, a fixed number of households is drawn in each cluster. Treating the data as a simple random sample gives the wrong estimates (no weights) and standard errors that are too small (no clustering). bdhs_design() sets the design up correctly for every round and recode.

This article uses synthetic data from bdhs_simulate(). The code is the same for your real data from bdhs_read().

The design in one line 

ir <- bdhs_simulate(2022, "IR")
des <- bdhs_design(ir)
des
#> Stratified 1 - level Cluster Sampling design (with replacement)
#> With (40) clusters.
#> bdhs_design(ir)

bdhs_design() detects the round and recode and then chooses:

  • PSU: the cluster, v021 (hv021 in household files, mv021 for men).
  • Strata: the DHS sampling-error strata, v022. The DHS Program recommends these for variance estimation in every round.
  • Weight: v005 / 1e6. DHS weights are stored as integers with six implied decimals.

bdhs_design_info() documents the design of each round, including its peculiarities:

info <- bdhs_design_info(recode = "IR")
info[, c("year_label", "psu", "strata", "weight", "n_strata", "strata_type")]
#> # A tibble: 9 × 6
#>   year_label psu   strata weight n_strata strata_type                           
#>   <chr>      <chr> <chr>  <chr>     <int> <chr>                                 
#> 1 1993-94    v021  v022   v005        148 paired-PSU sampling-error strata      
#> 2 1996-97    v021  v022   v005        154 paired-PSU sampling-error strata      
#> 3 1999-2000  v021  v022   v005        168 paired-PSU sampling-error strata      
#> 4 2004       v021  v022   v005        177 paired-PSU sampling-error strata      
#> 5 2007       v021  v022   v005        179 paired-PSU sampling-error strata      
#> 6 2011       v021  v022   v005         20 division x residence (city corporatio…
#> 7 2014       v021  v022   v005         20 division x residence (city corporatio…
#> 8 2017-18    v021  v022   v005         22 division x residence (city corporatio…
#> 9 2022       v021  v022   v005         16 division x urban/rural

A few points worth knowing:

  • Up to 2007, v022 holds 148 to 179 values with about two clusters each. These are the paired-cluster strata the DHS used for its sampling-error tables, and they are still the right choice. From 2011 the strata are the division x residence design strata (20 in 2011 and 2014, 22 in 2017-18, 16 in 2022).
  • strata = "design" uses v023 instead, and strata = "region_residence" rebuilds the strata from division and residence. Both are offered for sensitivity checks.

Estimating

Use the survey package (or srvyr) on the design:

svymean(~v201, des)
#>        mean     SE
#> v201 3.5713 0.1092
svyby(~v201, ~v025, des, svymean)
#>   v025     v201        se
#> 1    1 3.534211 0.1695193
#> 2    2 3.606190 0.1402556

For named DHS indicators, bdhs_estimate() builds the design for you and returns tidy estimates. See vignette("indicators").

Subgroups: subset the design, not the data

Filtering the data before building the design drops clusters and gives wrong standard errors. Subset the design instead:

young <- subset(des, v012 < 25)
svymean(~v201, young)
#>        mean     SE
#> v201 1.1391 0.0642

Strata with a single PSU

Subgroup analyses sometimes leave a stratum with only one cluster, and the survey package then refuses to compute a variance. The standard fix, which also matches the DHS Program’s own software, is:

options(survey.lonely.psu = "adjust")

bdhs_design() tells you when this applies, and bdhs_estimate() handles it automatically.

Other weights

weight = Weight Use it for
"default" v005, hv005, mv005 Almost everything
"dv" d005 (md005 for men) Domestic violence module
"male" hv028 Men’s subsample in household files
"household" hv005 Household-level analyses of member files
a column name any weight Special subsamples, such as biomarkers 
pr <- bdhs_simulate(2022, "PR")
bdhs_design(pr, weight = "household")
#> Stratified 1 - level Cluster Sampling design (with replacement)
#> With (40) clusters.
#> bdhs_design(pr, weight = "household")

Ever-married samples and “all women” indicators

Every BDHS women’s sample consists of ever-married women aged 15-49. Estimates for “all women”, such as the percentage of women aged 20-24 who married before 18, need a denominator that includes never-married women. The DHS Program supplies all-woman factors for this purpose: awfactt (total), awfactu (urban/rural), awfactr (division), awfacte (education) and awfactw (wealth, from 2004). Each factor, divided by 100, says how many women of all marital statuses one ever-married woman stands for.

An all-women percentage is then a ratio estimate. The numerator comes from ever-married women, and the denominator is inflated by the factor:

ir$married_before_18 <- as.numeric(ir$v511 < 18)
ir$aw <- ir$awfactt / 100
des <- bdhs_design(ir)
svyratio(~married_before_18, ~aw, subset(des, v012 >= 20 & v012 <= 24))
#> Ratio estimator: svyratio.survey.design2(~married_before_18, ~aw, subset(des, 
#>     v012 >= 20 & v012 <= 24))
#> Ratios=
#>                          aw
#> married_before_18 0.4651413
#> SEs=
#>                           aw
#> married_before_18 0.03722989

Use the factor that matches the breakdown: awfactu for estimates by residence, awfactr by division, and so on. bdhs_estimate() does this for the indicators that need it. All-woman factors only apply to characteristics that never-married women cannot have, such as marriage or births. They cannot be used for literacy, media exposure and similar characteristics.

Pooling rounds

bdhs_pool() stacks rounds, adds a survey_id column and builds a pooled weight pool_wt. bdhs_design() then gives every round its own strata and clusters:

pooled <- bdhs_pool(bdhs_simulate(2014, "IR"), bdhs_simulate(2022, "IR"), weights = "denormalized")
#> ℹ Value labels differ between rounds for 3 columns; kept the codes and dropped
#>   the labels: `v022`, `v023`, and `v024`.
#> ℹ DHS codes are not always comparable across rounds; use `harmonize = TRUE` or
#>   `bdhs_harmonize()` for comparable variables.
table(pooled$survey_id)
#> 
#> BD2014DHS BD2022DHS 
#>       551       552
pdes <- bdhs_design(pooled)
svyby(~v201, ~survey_id, pdes, svymean)
#>           survey_id     v201        se
#> BD2014DHS BD2014DHS 3.420633 0.1122980
#> BD2022DHS BD2022DHS 3.571310 0.1091613

The three weighting choices are:

  • "normalized": the DHS weights as they are. Rounds count in proportion to their sample size.
  • "denormalized": weights scaled to the population each round represents, using the bundled bdhs_pool_population (UN WPP 2024 female population 15-49 times the proportion ever married). This is the DHS Program’s recommendation for pooled estimates that describe the population.
  • "equal": every round carries the same total weight.
bdhs_pool_population[, c("survey_id", "ref_year", "female_15_49", "n_women_sample")]
#> # A tibble: 9 × 4
#>   survey_id ref_year female_15_49 n_women_sample
#>   <chr>        <dbl>        <dbl>          <int>
#> 1 BD1994DHS    1994.     28096489           9640
#> 2 BD1997DHS    1997.     30782776           9127
#> 3 BD2000DHS    2000.     33689291          10544
#> 4 BD2004DHS    2004.     36965636          11440
#> 5 BD2007DHS    2007.     39019159          10996
#> 6 BD2011DHS    2012.     41427050          17842
#> 7 BD2014DHS    2015.     43360901          17863
#> 8 BD2017DHS    2018.     45459595          20127
#> 9 BD2022DHS    2023.     48342561          30078

Add harmonize = TRUE to make variables comparable across the pooled rounds first (see vignette("harmonization")).

srvyr

Prefer dplyr-style code? Ask for a tbl_svy:

library(srvyr, warn.conflicts = FALSE)
bdhs_design(ir, srvyr = TRUE) |>
  group_by(v025 = haven::as_factor(v025)) |>
  summarise(children = survey_mean(v201, vartype = "ci"))
#> # A tibble: 2 × 4
#>   v025  children children_low children_upp
#>   <fct>    <dbl>        <dbl>        <dbl>
#> 1 urban     3.53         3.18         3.88
#> 2 rural     3.61         3.32         3.90
